lead: An aircraft section is mostly thin sheet: skins about 1 to 3 mm thick, webs and stringer flanges a few millimetres. Thin walls allow big simplifications. The stress hardly changes across the thickness, so each wall can be drawn as its mid-line with a thickness t, and terms in t³ can be dropped. This chapter sets out those approximations, gives the sums that turn walls and stringers into I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub>, works out the section properties of an angle and of the Z-section used in the previous chapters, and says where simple bending theory stops being accurate.
prereq: You need: the parallel-axis theorem and σ = M y/I from symmetrical bending, and the product second moment from unsymmetrical bending.

blocks.text: A wall is thin when its thickness t is small compared with its length s; t/s below about 0.1 covers most skins, webs and stringer flanges. Then:

items: The direct stress is taken as uniform across t, and the wall is drawn as its mid-line.
Lengths are measured along the mid-line, and the small overlap of material at corners is ignored.
Terms in t² and t³ are dropped against terms in t. A wall therefore has no second moment about its own mid-line.
Stringers are replaced by booms: concentrated areas at their centroids, with no second moment of their own.

blocks.text: For a straight wall of length s and thickness t at angle θ to the x axis, the second moments about axes through its own centroid are:
I<sub>xx,0</sub> = t s³ sin²θ/12,   I<sub>yy,0</sub> = t s³ cos²θ/12,   I<sub>xy,0</sub> = t s³ sin θ cos θ/12
blocks.where: t and s in mm give mm⁴. A horizontal wall (θ = 0) has I<sub>xx,0</sub> = 0 and I<sub>yy,0</sub> = t s³/12; a vertical wall (θ = 90°) the reverse. For a curved wall the same idea becomes an integral along the mid-line, for example t r³ ∫sin²φ dφ for a circular arc of radius r.

items: Draw the mid-line, number the walls and booms, and choose any reference axes.
Find the centroid: x̄ = Σ a x/Σ a and ȳ = Σ a y/Σ a, where a is each wall area t s or boom area A.

For each wall, add its own term to the parallel-axis term about the centroid: I<sub>xx</sub> = Σ(I<sub>xx,0</sub> + a y<sub>c</sub>²), I<sub>yy</sub> = Σ(I<sub>yy,0</sub> + a x<sub>c</sub>²), I<sub>xy</sub> = Σ(I<sub>xy,0</sub> + a x<sub>c</sub> y<sub>c</sub>), where (x<sub>c</sub>, y<sub>c</sub>) is the wall centroid measured from the section centroid.
Add the booms: A y², A x² and A x y about the centroid.
Keep the signs of x<sub>c</sub> and y<sub>c</sub>: they decide the sign of I<sub>xy</sub>.

blocks.text: A table with one row per wall keeps the work clear and is what examiners expect. The same properties serve open and closed sections: the direct stress depends only on A, I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub>. Shear flow and torsion differ, and the chapter on structural idealisation in shear flow shows how skin areas are lumped into booms for shear analysis.

sections.h3: Where bending theory stops being accurate

blocks.text: Some syllabi ask for the applicability of bending theory. The thin-walled answer assumes plane sections, uniform stress across each wall and elastic material. Three effects break those assumptions in aircraft panels:

items: Shear lag: in a wide skin the direct stress is higher near the webs and lower midway between them, so the peak stress exceeds the beam value. Designers use an effective width.
Local buckling and crippling: a thin compressed wall buckles below yield and then carries less load; see the chapters on plate buckling and crippling stress.

blocks.text: Use the thin-walled answer for sizing and first stress estimates, then check it with tests or finite elements.

spec.aria: An L-shaped angle drawn as two thick mid-lines: a vertical leg of 80 millimetres and a horizontal leg of 40 millimetres meeting at the bottom-left corner. Dashed centroidal x and y axes cross at G, 6.67 millimetres right of and 26.67 millimetres above the corner. The vertical leg centroid sits at minus 6.67, plus 13.33 and the horizontal leg centroid at plus 13.33, minus 26.67 from G. A dotted principal u axis runs at 15.8 degrees. A panel lists area 240 square millimetres, I x x 170,667, I y y 32,000, I x y minus 42,667, I u 182,743 and I v 19,924 millimetres to the fourth.

examples.question: An unequal angle has a vertical leg 80 mm long and a horizontal leg 40 mm long (mid-line lengths from the corner), both 2 mm thick. Using the thin-wall approximations, find the centroid, I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub>, I<sub>xy</sub> and the principal second moments.
steps: Put the corner at the origin. Vertical leg: a = 2 × 80 = 160 mm², centroid (0, 40). Horizontal leg: a = 2 × 40 = 80 mm², centroid (20, 0). Total A = 240 mm².
Wall centroids from the section centroid: vertical leg (−6.67, +13.33) mm, horizontal leg (+13.33, −26.67) mm.
Fill the table: own term plus parallel-axis term for each wall (t³ terms dropped).
Sum: I<sub>xx</sub> = 170,667 mm⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 32,000 mm⁴, I<sub>xy</sub> = -42,667 mm⁴. I<sub>xy</sub> is negative because both wall centroids sit in the second and fourth quadrants.
examples.answer: Centroid (6.67, 26.67) mm from the corner; I<sub>xx</sub> = 170,667 mm⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 32,000 mm⁴, I<sub>xy</sub> = -42,667 mm⁴; principal values 182,743 and 19,924 mm⁴ at θ = 15.8°.

examples.question: Find I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub> of the Z-section used in the unsymmetrical bending and deflection chapters: web 100 mm (vertical), top flange 50 mm in +x, bottom flange 50 mm in −x, all 2 mm thick.
steps: The section is antisymmetric about the web centre, so the centroid is at the middle of the web. Each flange has a = 100 mm²; the web has a = 200 mm².
I<sub>xx</sub>: web own term 2 × 100³/12 = 166,667; flanges 2 × 100 × 50² = 500,000 (their own I<sub>xx,0</sub> is zero). I<sub>xx</sub> = 666,667 mm⁴.
I<sub>yy</sub>: web contributes nothing; each flange has own term 2 × 50³/12 = 20,833 plus 100 × 25² = 62,500. I<sub>yy</sub> = 2 × 83,333 = 166,667 mm⁴.
I<sub>xy</sub>: top flange centroid (25, 50) gives 100 × 25 × 50 = 125,000; bottom flange (−25, −50) gives another +125,000; the web's centroid is at the origin. I<sub>xy</sub> = +250,000 mm⁴.
examples.answer: I<sub>xx</sub> = 666,667 mm⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 166,667 mm⁴ and I<sub>xy</sub> = +250,000 mm⁴, the values used for the Z-section stresses and deflections.

traps: Giving a horizontal wall an I<sub>xx</sub> own term of t s³/12. Its own I<sub>xx</sub> is zero in the thin-wall approximation; t s³/12 belongs to I<sub>yy</sub>.
Leaving out the parallel-axis terms a y<sub>c</sub>² and a x<sub>c</sub> y<sub>c</sub> of offset walls. For the angle they make up half of I<sub>xx</sub> (85,333 of 170,667 mm⁴).
Losing the signs of x<sub>c</sub> and y<sub>c</sub> in I<sub>xy</sub>. A sign slip turns +42,667 into −42,667 and tilts every neutral axis the wrong way.
Mixing millimetres and metres inside I. Convert once, before squaring or cubing.
Assuming open and closed sections need different direct-stress formulas; only their shear and torsion differ.

quiz.q: State the thin-wall approximations used for section properties.
quiz.a: Stress uniform across t; walls drawn as mid-lines; corner overlaps ignored; t² and t³ terms dropped; stringers as booms with no own second moment.

quiz.q: Why can a wall's second moment about its own mid-line be dropped?
quiz.a: It is s t³/12, while its parallel-axis and along-the-wall terms are of order t s y² and t s³. With t/s below about 0.1 the t³ term is under a hundredth of the others.

quiz.q: A vertical web 80 mm long and 1.5 mm thick has its centroid on the x axis. Find its I<sub>xx</sub>.
quiz.a: I<sub>xx</sub> = t s³/12 = 1.5 × 80³/12 = 64,000 mm⁴; there is no parallel-axis term because y<sub>c</sub> = 0.

quiz.q: A closed rectangular box has mid-line width 100 mm, depth 60 mm and walls 2 mm thick. Find I<sub>xx</sub> with the thin-wall approximations.
quiz.a: Top and bottom walls: 2 × (100 × 2) × 30² = 360,000 mm⁴. Side walls: 2 × 2 × 60³/12 = 72,000 mm⁴. I<sub>xx</sub> = 432,000 mm⁴.

quiz.q: A wall 60 mm long and 1 mm thick lies at 30° to the x axis, with its centroid at the section centroid. Find its I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub>.
quiz.a: t s³/12 = 18,000 mm⁴. I<sub>xx</sub> = 18,000 sin²30° = 4,500 mm⁴; I<sub>yy</sub> = 18,000 cos²30° = 13,500 mm⁴; I<sub>xy</sub> = 18,000 sin 30° cos 30° = 7,794 mm⁴.

quiz.q: Why is the thin-walled bending stress often optimistic for a compressed upper wing panel?
quiz.a: Shear lag raises the stress near the webs above the beam value, and the thin skin buckles locally below yield and then sheds load to the stringers. The simple theory sees neither effect.

quiz.q: The angle of the worked example is turned so that the horizontal leg points in −x. What changes in I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub>?
quiz.a: I<sub>xx</sub> and I<sub>yy</sub> are unchanged (squares of distances), but every x<sub>c</sub> changes sign, so I<sub>xy</sub> becomes +42,667 mm⁴ and the principal axes tilt the other way.

beyond: Sizing codes run these sums inside optimisation loops that change skin and stringer thicknesses station by station. Finite element models check shear lag and buckling, and composite sections use modulus-weighted areas, where each wall counts in proportion to its own E. Search for "modulus-weighted section properties" and "shear lag effective width box beam".
